criteria.name: Real-World Impact
criteria.description: Solves a real problem at your organization and fits a problem statement.
levels: Emerging: Problem or value is not yet clear.
Strong: Solves a meaningful real-world need.
Standout: Addresses an important need with clear, significant value.

criteria.name: Staying Power
criteria.description: The team and their colleagues will keep using it; a reusable skill, agent, MCP integration, or workflow.
levels: Strong: Has potential to continue with additional development.
Standout: Clear path to ongoing use, adoption, or scale.

criteria.name: Claude Code Craft
criteria.description: Creative, unique use of Claude Code beyond a single prompt.
levels: Emerging: Basic use of Claude Code.
Strong: Claude Code is used effectively to build the solution.
Standout: Creative and thoughtful use of Claude Code that meaningfully improves the solution.

criteria.name: Execution & Demo
criteria.description: Sound engineering, refined past the first idea, and a working demo that holds up live.
levels: Emerging: Early or incomplete; difficult to assess.
Strong: Working solution with a clear demo.
Standout: Polished, functional solution with a compelling demo.

scoring.notes: Judge Scorecard (primary): each judge scores every project from 1 (weak) to 10 (exceptional) on all four criteria. The four categories are weighted equally at 25%, so a project's final score is the simple sum of the four (maximum 40). Scoring guide: 1-3 Limited (little evidence of the criterion; concept stage or non-functional); 4-6 Solid (meets the criterion; works as shown with room to grow); 7-8 Strong (clearly exceeds expectations; polished and convincing); 9-10 Exceptional (best-in-show caliber; you would champion this project yourself). Judges enter project names in the order they demo, total each row in the Final Score column, and hand the completed scorecard to the organizer for tallying across judges. The earlier Hackathon Judging Rubric document uses a simpler 1-3 scale per category (Emerging / Strong / Standout, maximum 12) with a judge note field; the Judge Scorecard supersedes it for tallying. Tie-breaks are resolved in a judging huddle: for close calls, judges discuss which project delivers the strongest combination of real-world value, potential to continue beyond the hackathon, thoughtful use of Claude Code, and demonstrated execution. The rubric also lists three optional huddle call-outs: Best Real-World Scenario (most compelling or unexpected use case), Boldest Idea (most creative or ambitious concept), and Most Likely to Ship (solution people could imagine using soon). Neil and Xiaoxue plan to build an automated scoring system during the event to help synthesize submissions; the paper scorecard is the fallback.

toolkit.author: Neil Hausmann
toolkit.intro: Built on the day to support the judging huddle. The design goal running through all four pieces: turn judgment into something that can be questioned. Every band, every award and every superlative points at a slide number, a commit SHA or a measured number rather than a recollection.
toolkit.quote: The presentation is the submission's claim. The commits are its behaviour. Most mis-scoring is one of two errors: a polished deck reading as execution, or a strong commit history going unscored because the deck never showed it. Score the two channels separately and report where they disagree — that disagreement is usually the most informative thing about a submission.

items.name: collect_evidence.py
items.description: Reads a team's deck and their local git repos and emits one JSON evidence file. Scores nothing — it produces only citable facts: slide numbers, commit SHAs, file paths. Anything it cannot observe is emitted as null rather than guessed.

items.name: hackathon-judge skill
items.description: The Claude skill that scores a submission from its presentation and its git history together, on the Judge Scorecard 1-10 across four criteria, with the legacy 1-3 bands as the evidence anchor. Emits cited rationale and a confidence per score.

items.name: assign_awards.py
items.description: Assigns the superlative awards so every team gets exactly one, deterministically. Ranks teams on each metric and maximises how distinctive each team is on the award it receives, so no citation is a vibe. Carries ~28 alternative prizes; rubric winners are excluded by default.

items.name: fetch_control_tower.py
items.description: Polls this Control Tower for the roster and submissions and reports what changed since the last poll — which team just attached a deck, a repo or a video. Has a watch mode for use during the event.

results.source: Judge card from Neil Hausmann, produced with the judging toolkit below.
results.caveat: This is ONE judge's scorecard, not the tallied panel result. It ranks awards by how well the evidence supports them: ranks 1-6 were put forward as decided, 7-9 went to the huddle as open questions. Ceremony order deliberately differed, running the prestige awards last.
results.scale: 1-10 per criterion across four criteria, maximum 40. The legacy 1-3 band view (max 12) is kept alongside as the evidence anchor.

slate.why: The longest commit message in the field at 1,751 characters - from the team named Git Blame. The joke lands because it inverts their own name: instead of blame being a mystery you have to excavate, they wrote the explanation directly into the history. They lead the field by 1.7 standard deviations.
slate.challenge: None. Measured from the commit log, unique leader, independently re-runnable.

slate.basis: 'The best tools know when to stop'
slate.why: Their tool's headline feature is declining to act. It turns whiteboard photos and meeting transcripts into Jira tickets and REFUSES to write the vague ones - asking at most three questions, ranked by blast radius, and holding a ticket as a ghost until the ambiguity blocking it is resolved. 'A held ticket is an output, not a failure.' The guardrails are deterministic C#, deliberately not entrusted to model output. No other submission is designed around a refusal.
slate.challenge: None. Verbatim from their own deck; no other submission is refusal-first.

slate.why: The richest harness in the field, and the only one whose gates I could actually execute. Four subagents with exclusive file ownership working against contracts frozen by a PreToolUse hook that BLOCKS rather than advises; post-edit hooks that re-run the rule tests and a data-invariant check after every single edit; and a project-specific /add-rule skill so someone who is not the original author can add rule seventeen. Their documented before/after is unflattering and therefore credible: a secret scanner that passed FALSELY on Windows (decoding nine files as empty) was replaced with assertions about the data itself. I ran their suite - 308 tests pass - and their invariant gate green.
slate.challenge: 'Why not A or Journey at 8?' P is the only harness I could EXECUTE. Repo-channel citations only, so not HIGH.

slate.why: The clearest and most carefully-bounded statement of value in the field. An affordability map for prospective students, built around undocumented and mixed-status students: no account, no email, no SSN, and it never asks immigration status, birthplace or address - a constraint sourced to NILC, ACLU and the Presidents' Alliance. Skipping any question WIDENS the estimate rather than blocking you. And it refuses to oversell itself: real sourced aid rules are separated from illustrative dollar placeholders, and an unsettled Texas in-state tuition case is surfaced as uncertainty rather than guessed.
slate.challenge: Advocacy-guidance citation is unverifiable (the design choices ARE directly observed in the code).

slate.why: The only deck that footnoted its own numbers. It answers a question a real person actually asks - 'where does Math Pathways show up in A&SI, and what are the outcomes and dollars?' - with $26.9M approved / $24.1M paid across 17 investments (8 active, 9 closed), and then states the provenance on the slide: 'SIP snapshot 2026-08-13, inbound budget (FundsToBoW) + lifetime investment totals, PRI excluded.' Naming the snapshot date and the exclusion rule is what separates a scenario that is compelling from one that is merely plausible.
slate.challenge: Judged category with three plausible claimants (K, S, R). K's discriminator - footnoting its own snapshot date and exclusion rule - is observed and rare.

slate.why: Two of its integrations are already real rather than mocked: it pulls new AI Engagement records from the live Airtable tracker (additive only, never overwriting prior imports), and accepting a connector request creates an actual Ardoq Connector Technology Service component with an initial 'Evaluating' lifecycle phase, linking requesting and providing systems where an unambiguous match already exists. Eight test files back it. Everything else is deliberately mocked so nothing leaves the machine - the boundary is drawn honestly and documented.
slate.challenge: 'Isn't O more likely to ship - it is already deployed?' Yes. O is excluded because it holds Built to Last. Policy, not evidence.

slate.why: The broadest submission in the field - the only one with no weak criterion (8/8/8/6). A daily Gearset triage agent that reads the failure card from Teams, opens the Jira bug BEFORE any analysis so a failure always leaves a tracked ticket rather than nothing, root-causes merge-aware, and stops at a draft PR. Its problem statement is measured and dated rather than asserted: 28% of recent commits are merges and 9% are bot commits, so blame lands on noise instead of the change that broke the test - and the agent's merge-aware design answers exactly that finding. It ships in REPORT_ONLY with a stated ramp to full autonomy only after its reports earn trust.
slate.challenge: 'P scored 31.' A holds it only because P took Wizardry. A's 30 is also the score revised most (17 -> 30, after finding their deck in Assets/ and skill in .claude/) and the least re-verified.

slate.basis: Mine the failure data you already have
slate.why: The insight is that support teams already own the data that predicts their own failures - Jira stories, linked bugs, QA defects, Salesforce metadata - and nobody mines it. Rather than writing knowledge-base articles from scratch, it drafts from failures that have ALREADY occurred, walks 14 failure categories and explicitly rules one out rather than skipping it silently, and enforces 'cite or don't write it' so every step traces to a Jira key or metadata component with no invented UI. Draft-only: every output goes to SME review before it reaches an agent.
slate.challenge: Near coin-flip against R, whose refuse-to-write is arguably bolder. Two deck-only submissions, no discriminating evidence.

slate.why: The only submission already deployed and independently verified - I confirmed in the workspace that the app is ACTIVE and was updated at 21:33Z during the event, by a member of this team. It is built to outlive the demo: a numbered SQL migration (001_create_schema.sql), app.yaml, .env.example, a seed-data loader, and most importantly an on-behalf-of auth model that uses the caller's own OAuth token from x-forwarded-access-token rather than service-principal credentials. That means row-level permissions follow the real user, and a colleague can use it tomorrow with no credentials of their own.
slate.challenge: Four-way tie at 8; two excluded; O vs Journey have equal confidence, comparable corroboration and IDENTICAL totals (28). Stated tiebreaks all exhausted - decided on judgment alone.
